final_answer:
No. The trial court did not err; disqualification was proper (and, on these facts, the Texas Supreme Court has denied mandamus relief against an essentially identical disqualification order). The fact pattern tracks In re Zaidi, No. 24-0245 (Tex. Apr. 10, 2026) (Devine, J.) (Prestige Consulting d/b/a Turnaround Management Group as relator), which I could verify only through search-result summaries (the opinion PDF and reporters were blocked by the network proxy).

Rule. Texas disqualifies lawyers and firms through the disciplinary rules as guidelines and the Supreme Court's common law. For a nonlawyer (paralegal/legal assistant) who switches sides, Phoenix Founders, Inc. v. Marshall, 887 S.W.2d 831 (Tex. 1994), In re American Home Products Corp., 985 S.W.2d 68 (Tex. 1998), and In re Columbia Valley Healthcare System, L.P., 320 S.W.3d 819 (Tex. 2010), establish: (1) an irrebuttable presumption that the nonlawyer obtained confidences from the former employer's client; (2) a rebuttable presumption that the nonlawyer shared them with the new firm; (3) the presumption of sharing is rebutted only if the new firm shows it timely and effectively screened the nonlawyer; and (4) where the nonlawyer worked on the SAME matter for the opposing side, the rule is strict: the new firm must instruct the employee, at or before the start of employment on that matter, not to work on or discuss the matter, and take reasonable steps (barring access to files, etc.), and it must strictly adhere to those measures. Where the nonlawyer actually discloses confidences, or the firm fails to take the prophylactic measures, the entire firm is disqualified. In re Turner, 542 S.W.3d 553 (Tex. 2017) (applying the same framework to a paralegal who worked on the same matter at both firms; screening there was effective and disqualification denied because the firm screened immediately upon learning of the conflict).

Application. Jones plainly was a side-switcher on the same matter: 2009-2011 she prepared litigation documents, took part in several hundred privileged communications and strategy meetings for Apex, so the presumption that she acquired confidences is irrebuttable. Smith Fullingham did nothing at hire (no inquiry), nothing when she first worked on the matter in 2017, and nothing during thirteen occasions of work through 2022, culminating in her e-filing in her name in March 2022; it first announced a screen only after Apex's inquiry in January 2023. Because the firm gave no instruction or screen at or before the time she began work on the conflicted matter, the presumption of shared confidences cannot be rebutted. Zaidi squarely rejects the arguments the firm would raise: (a) that she was not a side-switcher when hired and the conflict arose years later (the duty to instruct attaches when the employee begins work on the conflicted matter, even years after hire; a firm's failure to inquire into the new hire's prior work is its own risk); (b) that her work was minimal or secretarial (the rule does not turn on how much she did); and (c) that she did not recall the prior work or no actual confidences were shared (the presumptions are not defeated by testimony of non-recollection or denials; a late screen is ineffective). The firm's after-the-fact screen in 2023 comes too late, and the firm bears the burden of proving effective screening.

Waiver. Disqualification can be waived by unreasonable delay, but the movant's delay is measured from when it knew or should have known of the conflict, with the opponent bearing a heavy burden (Vaughan v. Walther, 875 S.W.2d 690 (Tex. 1994); In re EPIC Holdings, 985 S.W.2d 41 (Tex. 1998)). Apex first learned of Jones's employment in January 2023 from a filing notification, asked the firm, and moved within about two months (early March 2023). Zaidi held, as a matter of law, that the movant did not waive by delay in a nearly identical posture (an e-filing notice bearing the legal assistant's name does not by itself put the former client on notice of a conflict or start the clock for years before). The 2011-2017 period and the March 2022 e-filing do not establish waiver; a month-or-two of investigation is reasonable; also no tactical abuse is shown.

Standard of review. Disqualification orders are reviewed for abuse of discretion, and mandamus is the proper vehicle; a trial court that misapplies the law abuses its discretion. Here the court applied the law correctly.

Conclusion. Disqualification of the whole firm was correct; the firm's only way to avoid it (timely, strictly maintained screening) was not available. Caveat: I could not read the full Zaidi opinion; specific holdings about waiver and the e-filing notice come from secondary summaries and should be verified, as should the Turner and Columbia Valley pinpoints.

claims.text: Jones's prior work on the same matter for Apex creates an irrebuttable presumption she obtained confidences and a rebuttable presumption she shared them with Smith Fullingham.

Because the firm did not instruct/screen her at or before she began work on the matter, even years after hire, the presumption is not rebutted and the firm is disqualified; a late 2023 screen and non-recollection do not cure.
Apex did not waive: it moved within about two months of learning of her employment, and the e-filing notice did not as a matter of law establish waiver.
The trial court therefore did not abuse its discretion in disqualifying the firm.
